new_statements.quote: [p. 263] Stress is not phonemic. It tends to fall on the first vowel of a word but it is bound to the morphemes of the imperative and vocative (ylỳj, ylà 'father!'; přyjà 'come!') and is very frequently associated with certain emphatic verbal morphemes (přy=nd=rà 'he came, indeed'). [p. 277, on nursery words] Stress falls, as it does in standard words, on the first vowel; certain reduplicated forms may carry it on the second vowel (40, 46, 51, 53, 54). [p. 268 n. 2] There are also two (standard) imperatives: :j/i (where : = stressed stem-final vowel) and jà

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog carries Sakhalin Nivkh with an empty rule and no existing statements; Austerlitz supplies the placement (non-phonemic, default first vowel) plus the morphological exceptions. It agrees with the consensus that Shiraishi 2002 (already held by the project from an earlier reading, not in this work list) attributes to Austerlitz 1956: 263, Bondarko & Zinder 1962, Panfilov 1962 and Hattori 1988 ('accent is placed on the leftmost syllable in Nivkh'). new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and falls by default on the first vowel (first syllable) of the word; it is displaced to the vocative/imperative morphemes (word-final in the examples, marked with a grave: ylỳj, ylà, přyjà) and very often to emphatic verbal morphemes such as =rà. In nursery words the same initial default holds, but some reduplicated forms carry stress on the second vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Vocative and imperative morphemes attract stress (ylỳj / ylà 'father!', přyjà 'come!'; imperative :j/i with the stem-final vowel stressed, p. 268 n. 2); certain emphatic verbal morphemes are 'very frequently' stressed (přy=nd=rà); in nursery vocabulary certain reduplicated forms carry stress on the second vowel (items 40, 46, 51, 53, 54). Vowel quantity is contrastive only in numerals and a few morphemes (tōχ, ī).
new_statements.identity_note: Austerlitz 1956 describes 'the dialect of southeastern Sakhalin in the idiolect of the informant' (p. 261): Mrs. Tiyoko Nakamura, born 1906 near Siska (Poronaysk area), south-eastern Sakhalin, daughter of a Tungus (Sandan) father and a Gilyak mother, resident in Abashiri, Hokkaido since 1949; data collected 1954-56. This is East Sakhalin Nivkh and falls under sakh1247 (Sakhalin Nivkh); it is not the Amur variety. Footnote 12 (p. 277) also cites a 'West-coast Sakhalin form' for one verb, but no stress claim is attached to it.

tone.quote: 2.5. 強勢 Gruzdeva (1998: 12) によれば、ニヴフ語ではどの音節にも強勢が落ちることがあるが、第1 音節に落ちる傾向がある。さらに、Krejnovič (1979: 298-299) は、複合語においてはその内部構造によって違うパターンを示すと述べており、サハリン方言においては 2 つ以上の名詞語幹からできている複合語の場合は、最後の語幹に強勢が落ち、名詞＋動詞の複合語の場合は名詞語幹に強勢が落ちるという。筆者の調査によると、東サハリン方言においては、原則として第一音節に強勢が落ちる。(82) Krejnovič (1979: 298-299) [vs] 筆者の調査結果: amámnt「歩く」 ámamt; vuk~vukúnt「暗い」 vúk~vukt; teŋí「カラフトマス」 téŋi; raúnt「教える」 ráwut [...] [p. 12:] 語アクセントは、原則的に第一音節に落ちる。場合によっては、母音が長く発音されることがあるが音韻的な対立をなすものではない。
tone.locator: sec. 2.5 強勢, p. 52, with example (82); plus ch. 1 grammatical overview, p. 12
tone.translation: 2.5 Stress. According to Gruzdeva (1998: 12), stress in Nivkh may fall on any syllable but tends to fall on the first. Further, Krejnovic (1979: 298-299) states that compounds show different patterns depending on their internal structure: in the Sakhalin dialect a compound of two or more noun stems is stressed on the last stem, a noun+verb compound on the noun stem. According to the author's own fieldwork, in the East Sakhalin dialect stress falls, as a rule, on the first syllable. (82) Krejnovic's forms vs the author's results: amámnt 'walk' vs ámamt; vuk~vukúnt 'dark' vs vúk~vukt; teŋí 'pink salmon' vs téŋi; raúnt 'teach' vs ráwut ... [p. 12, grammatical overview:] Word accent falls in principle on the first syllable. In some cases a vowel is pronounced long, but this does not constitute a phonological opposition.
